questions.explain: Conjugating psi's entries gives 2+i and -i. Term 1: (2+i)(1+i) = 1+3i. Term 2: (-i)(3) = -3i. Summing: (1+3i) + (-3i) = 1, with the imaginary parts cancelling exactly.

questions.q: The Pauli Y matrix M = [[0,-i],[i,0]] is checked for the Hermitian property. What is the result, and what does it predict about its eigenvalues?
options: M is Hermitian (real diagonal, and off-diagonal entries -i and i are conjugates of each other), so its eigenvalues must be real -- confirmed as lambda = +1 and -1
M is not Hermitian because its diagonal entries are both zero
M fails the Hermitian test because -i and i are not conjugates of each other
M is Hermitian, but this guarantees nothing about whether its eigenvalues are real
questions.explain: Both diagonal entries (0, 0) are real, and (-i)* = i matches M_21 exactly, so M is Hermitian. Solving trace=0, det=-1 gives eigenvalues +1 and -1, both real, exactly as the Hermitian-implies-real-eigenvalues theorem predicts.

questions.q: For N = (1/sqrt(2))[[1,i],[i,1]], computing N^dagger N gives the identity matrix I. What happens if you mistakenly drop the 1/sqrt(2) normalizing factor and test [[1,i],[i,1]] directly?
options: The result is still exactly I, since the normalizing factor doesn't affect unitarity
The result becomes the zero matrix, since removing the normalization cancels everything
The result becomes 2I instead of I, so the unnormalized matrix fails the unitary test even though its structure looks almost identical
The matrix becomes Hermitian instead of unitary
questions.explain: Without the 1/sqrt(2) factor, the same entry-by-entry multiplication gives [[2,0],[0,2]] = 2I, not I -- a matrix that looks deceptively similar but is not unitary. This is exactly why the lab warns to always check the result equals I exactly.

questions.q: For |psi> = (1/sqrt(2))(1,1) and |phi> = (1,0), computing |<psi|phi>|^2 gives 1/2. What does this value represent in the quantum computing interpretation previewed in this chapter?
options: The exact energy of the qubit in joules
The probability of measuring a qubit prepared in the equal-superposition state |psi> and finding it in state |0>, which comes out to a clean 50 percent
The angle in degrees between |psi> and |phi> in ordinary 3D space
The number of gates required to prepare the state |psi>
questions.explain: |<psi|phi>|^2 previews the Born-rule idea: for a normalized state, this quantity gives a measurement probability. Here it works out to 1/2, matching the intuition that an equal superposition should give a 50/50 measurement outcome.

questions.q: This lab's four problems reuse concepts from which earlier lessons in this chapter, without introducing any new theory?
options: Inner products (Lesson 21), Hermitian operators (Lesson 22), unitary operators (Lesson 23), and the probability-style interpretation of inner products tied to orthonormal bases (Lessons 21 and 24)
Only matrix determinants and matrix inverses from Chapter 2
Entirely new theory not covered in any previous lesson in this course
Only the complex number arithmetic from Chapter 3, with no connection to operators at all
questions.explain: The lab is explicitly built as reinforcement: each problem runs the exact test introduced in one of this chapter's four theory lessons (inner product, Hermitian check, unitary check, probability interpretation) on fresh numbers, with no new concepts introduced.
